passage: I'm Vidya, and this is about the week my son Raghav sounded low. He had moved to Kolkata for his hotel-management course, and on Thursday his voice was flat. 'The food's fine, Amma,' he said, and it clearly wasn't. After I hung up I sat in his empty room and cried, and I wanted so badly to say, come home, we'll find a college here. My sister said I should tell him how much I was suffering. I didn't. Instead I called every evening at nine, just ten minutes, never asking when he'd be back. I told him about the neighbour's new calf and the mango pickle I was sending. By the second week he laughed at the calf story. I still miss him terribly. But I think he needed a home to lean on, not a door to walk back through.

qa.q: What time did Vidya call Raghav each evening?
qa.a: At nine, for just ten minutes.

qa.q: What did Vidya want to say after the Thursday call, and why didn't she?
qa.a: She wanted to tell him to come home because she missed him and was worried, but she held back so he could keep growing there.

qa.q: Why was Vidya's way of calling a good choice?
qa.a: Short, warm, regular calls with no guilt and no questions about returning gave Raghav a steady base while he found his feet.

qa.q: What might Raghav feel on hearing the calf story?
qa.a: Raghav may feel comforted and connected to home, able to laugh again without feeling pulled back.

grounding: Shows a parent at home feeling the child's absence and worry, and choosing warm regular calls without guilt or demands to return.

passage:
Student Wellbeing Cell, note, 14 August.
Tejas, first year, came in after his father, Mr Hrithik Joshi, phoned the hostel office twice in one day. Tejas said his father had heard him sounding low on Sunday and panicked. With Tejas's permission I spoke to Mr Joshi on speaker. He said the house had felt too quiet since Tejas left, and he had been setting three plates at dinner out of habit. He admitted he had told Tejas, 'If you're unhappy, just come back, why suffer?' and then felt guilty when Tejas went silent. We talked about calls that keep the door warm without pulling. He agreed to a fixed Sunday call and to ask about Tejas's day, not about returning. Tejas looked relieved. Next steps: emailed Mr Joshi our short guide for parents; will check in with Tejas in two weeks.

qa.q: What had Mr Joshi been doing at dinner out of habit?
qa.a: Setting three plates.

qa.q: How did Mr Joshi feel after telling Tejas to just come back?
qa.a: He felt guilty when Tejas went silent, sensing that his worry had turned into pressure.

qa.q: What change was agreed to help both of them?
qa.a: A fixed Sunday call in which Mr Joshi asks about Tejas's day rather than about returning, so Tejas keeps a base without being pulled home.

qa.q: What might Tejas have felt hearing his father say the house felt too quiet?
qa.a: Tejas may have felt touched and a little guilty, then relieved once the calls were set up without pressure to come back.

grounding: Illustrates a parent at home missing a son who sounds low, first pulling him back and then agreeing to warm, regular calls without demands.

passage:
The power went out in Shillong just as Elizabeth dialled her son. The phone had eight per cent battery.

"Mama?" Kamal's voice from Pune was flat. "I'm fine. Just tired."

Elizabeth had heard that flatness three calls in a row. Her chest tightened. The old words rose up: Come home, this was a mistake, who told you to go so far. She held them.

"Tired how?" she asked instead, watching the candle.

"Nobody here says my name right. The food is... I don't know, Mama."

"I miss you too," she said. "Your chair looks very empty." Then, carefully: "Tell me one thing that wasn't bad today."

A pause. "The college canteen had momos. Terrible momos."

She laughed. The battery flashed red. "Sunday, same time? I'll charge the phone."

"Sunday," he said, and he sounded a little less tired.

qa.q: How much battery did Elizabeth's phone have?
qa.a: The phone had eight per cent battery.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she heard the flatness in Kamal's voice?
qa.a: She felt worried and anxious, with a strong pull to tell him to come home, which she chose to hold back.

qa.q: Which choice worked in this call, and why?
qa.a: Elizabeth asked gently and said she missed him without guilt, then set a regular Sunday call, giving Kamal a warm base while he stays.

qa.q: How is Kamal affected by the way his mother handled the call?
qa.a: Kamal seemed a little lighter by the end, able to share something small and knowing he could count on Sunday.

grounding: A parent at home feels the child's absence and worry, and responds with warm, regular calls without guilt-tripping or demanding a return.

passage:
In the Kochi flat, Francis set two cups of tea on the table out of habit before remembering that Tushar was in Delhi.

Their Sunday call came at eight, as always. Tushar's face on the screen looked thinner.

"Hostel food," he said, when Francis asked. "It's fine, Pappa."

Francis heard what wasn't fine. His hand went to the second cup. He wanted to say, Your mother cried twice this week. You don't have to stay there. Instead he said, "The mango tree has fruit. Mummy is making pickle. I'll courier a jar."

Tushar smiled for the first time. "The spicy one?"

"The spicy one."

After the call, Francis stayed at the table for a long time. The empty chair was hard. But Tushar had laughed, and a jar of pickle was something he could actually do.

qa.q: What was Mummy making?
qa.a: Mummy was making pickle.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when his hand went to the second cup?
qa.a: He felt the ache of missing his son and a pull to tell him to come home, which he held back.

qa.q: What made Francis's response a helpful one?
qa.a: He didn't guilt-trip or ask Tushar to return; he shared warm news from home and offered something practical, the pickle, which kept home close.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel after this call?
qa.a: Tushar likely feels comforted and connected to home, especially at the thought of the spicy pickle.

grounding: A parent feels the absence and worries when the child sounds low, choosing warmth over guilt-tripping or demands to return.

passage:
"Ammi, I'm fine."

"You said that yesterday too, Shankar. In the same voice."

"The mess food is bad. My roommate snores. Nobody here speaks Urdu. It's all fine."

Farida switched the phone to her other ear and sat down on the kitchen stool. "I made your seviyan today. Out of habit. Your Abba ate two bowls, pretending it was for him."

"Don't, Ammi, you'll make me miss home more."

"Good. You should miss home. Home misses you." She paused. "But I'm not asking you to come back. I'm asking you to call me every evening at nine, even if it's for two minutes."

"Every evening?"

"Two minutes. Tell me one thing you saw. That's all."

A long breath from Hyderabad. "Today I saw a man selling cats' toys on a bicycle."

"Now that," said Farida, "is a good thing to tell your mother."

qa.q: What did Farida make today?
qa.a: She made Shankar's seviyan, out of habit.

qa.q: What might Farida be worried about as she sits down on the kitchen stool?
qa.a: She is worried that Shankar is lonely and low, since he keeps saying he's fine in the same flat voice.

qa.q: What small step did Farida suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: A two-minute call every evening at nine; it gives Shankar a steady link to home without pressure to return.

qa.q: How is Shankar affected by his mother's approach?
qa.a: Shankar is touched but a little embarrassed at first, then relaxes enough to share a funny detail from his day.

grounding: A dialogue shows a parent feeling the child's absence and offering regular warm calls, without guilt or demands to return.

passage: I'm Hrithik. In my first term at college in Bengaluru, I called home one Sunday and couldn't hide how flat I sounded. Papa heard it straight away. "You're tired, beta?" I said I was fine. Later, Ma told me he'd sat on the balcony for an hour after that call, not saying much. I didn't know parents missed you like that. After that, Papa called every Sunday at eight. He never said "come home" or "we're so lonely without you." He asked what I ate, whether my roommate Deepak still snored, how the chemistry lab went. Sometimes he'd send a photo of the neighbour's cat on our wall. I knew he was worried; he just didn't make it my job to fix. Looking back, those calls were like a rope I could hold. I stayed, I settled, and I still knew exactly where home was.

qa.q: At what time did Papa call every Sunday?
qa.a: Papa called every Sunday at eight.

qa.q: What does Papa sitting on the balcony for an hour suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests Papa felt worried and sad, missing his child and anxious after hearing Hrithik sound low.

qa.q: What made Papa's calls helpful rather than heavy?
qa.a: They were regular and warm, asked about daily things, and carried no guilt-tripping or demands to return, so Hrithik could settle while keeping a base.

qa.q: How might the calls have been different if Papa had said we're so lonely without you?
qa.a: Hrithik might have felt guilty and torn about staying, making it harder to settle in Bengaluru.

grounding: Shows parents feeling a child's absence and worrying when the young person sounds low, and a parent's regular, warm calls without guilt or pressure giving the young person a base.
